Divergent Reactivity of δ- and β′-Acetoxy Allenoates with
2‑Sulfonamidoindoles via Phosphine Catalysis: Entry to Dihydro- α-
carboline, α‑Carboline, and Spiro-cyclopentene Motifs
Shubham Debnath, # A. Sanjeeva Kumar, # Sachin Chauhan, and K. C. Kumara Swamy *
Cite This: J. Org. Chem. 2021, 86, 11583 −11598 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: The reactivity of 2-sulfonamidoindoles with acetoxy allenoates under phosphine catalysis depends on the disposition
of the acetoxy (OAc) group on the allenoate. In the temperature-controlled [3 + 3] annulations, δ-acetoxy allenoates a ﬀorded
dihydrocarboline and carboline sca ﬀolds with carbon −nitrogen nucleophilic 2-sulfonamidoindoles, in which allenoate serves as a β-,
γ-, and δ-carbon donor. At room temperature (25 °C), dihydro- α-carboline motifs were obtained exclusively through Michael
addition, 1,4-proton shift, isomerization, 1,2-proton transfer, phosphine elimination, and aza-Michael addition. The higher
temperature (80 °C) cascade protocol using Ph
3P−Cs2CO3 combination involves addition −elimination, aza-Claisen rearrangement,
tosyl migration, and aromatization as key steps to give α-carbolines containing tosyl f unctionality at the γ-carbon. In contrast, with β′-
acetoxy allenoate, 2-sulfonamidoindole acts only as a carbo-nucleophile in ( p-tolyl)3P-directed [4 + 1] spiro-annulation, leading to
ﬁve-membered spiro-carbocyclic motifs essentially as single diastereomers (dr >20:1) via chemoselective carbo-annulation.
■ INTRODUCTION
Over the past few decades, transformations involving allenes
have evolved as powerful tools in organic synthesis. 1,2 Since the
discovery of Lu ’s [3 + 2] cycloaddition of allenoates using
phosphine,3 numerous Lewis base-catalyzed/mediated annula-
tions of allenoates have been reported. 4,5 Later, acetoxy
allenoates were widely utilized as useful synthons in a variety
of annulations by Tong as well as other groups. 6,7 Generally,
the nucleophilic attack of Lewis base at sp-hybridized carbon
generates a zwitterionic intermediate, which is then trapped in
situ with other partners. These annulations are demonstrated
as reliable approaches in organic synthesis leading to a wide
array of carbo- and heterocycles ( Scheme 1 ). Tong and co-
workers reported a [3 + 3] annulation with δ-acetoxy allenoate
functioning as 3C-synthon ( α-, β-, and γ-carbons participated)
using phosphine ( Scheme 1 b).8a Subsequently, Tong ’s8b,e and
Shi’s8c groups successfully explored [3 + 2] annulations
(Scheme 1 c) of δ-acetoxy allenoates with 1C, 2/3N
binucleophiles using phosphine; these reactions were facili-
tated by the addition of nucleophile at the δ-carbon of diene-
phosphonium intermedi ate. In 2017, the Tong ’sg r o u p
reported the reaction between δ-acetoxy allenoate and 2-
naphthol in which allenoate acted as a 2C ( γ and δ) synthon,
but in the case of 1-naphthol, the allenoate acted as both a 2C
(γ and δ) and 3C- ( α, β, and γ) synthon and led to ﬁve- as well
as six-membered oxacycles ( Scheme 1 d).8d Very recently,
Zhou’s group 8f reported a domino [3 + 2] and [3 + 2]
annulation protocol involving δ-acetoxy allenoate as a 2C-
synthon ( γ, δ or β, γ) to synthesize a fused six-membered
heterocyclic core with an exocyclic double bond ( Scheme 1e).
Apart from these, previously, Tong ’s group reported the ﬁrst
example of [4 + 1] annulation using a β′-acetoxy allenoate
leading to a ﬁve-membered carbocyclic motif ( Scheme 1 f)

under phosphine catalysis. 9a Subsequently, others also
employed β′-acetoxy allenoate in numerous [4 + 1]
annulations,9b−e but spiro-carbo annulations are scarce. 9f
However, to the best of our knowledge, [3 + 3] annulation
involving β-, γ-, and δ-carbons of δ-acetoxy allenoates as well as
f unctional group migration using phosphine has not been
reported until now.
Previously, 2-sulfonamidoindoles have been used as versatile
building blocks for the construction of six-/seven-membered
aza-heterocyclic cores ( Scheme 2 a,b),10 but not for the
generation of the spirocyclic motifs or 1,2-dihydrocarbolines.
Spirocyclic quaternary stereocenters have gained a great deal of
attention in organic synthesis
11 and often appear in bioactive
compounds,12 while α-carbolines are encountered in a variety
of bioactive molecules. 13 As a part of our continued interest in
the reactions of allenes, 1g,6c,d,14 herein we disclose chemo-
selective [3 + 3]-hetero- and [4 + 1] spiro-carbo-annulations of
2-sulfonamidoindoles with acetoxy allenoates that highlight (i)
Ph
3P-catalyzed temperature-dependent [3 + 3] heteroannula-
tions of δ-acetoxy allenoates a ﬀording a novel class of dihydro-
α-carboline and α-carboline motifs, the latter via tosyl
migration to the γ-carbon, in which sulfonomidoindole acts
as a C/N-donor and (ii) ( p-tolyl)3P-catalyzed [4 + 1] spiro-
carbo-annulation of β′-acetoxy allenoates leading to spirocy-
clopentene motifs with excellent stereoselectivity (dr up to
20:1).
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
To optimize the reaction conditions, we explored the reaction
of 2-sulfonamidoindole 1a with δ-acetoxy allenoate 2a. The
results are collated in Table 1 . Initially, we tested the reaction
between 1a (0.20 mmol) and 2a (0.24 mmol) in the presence
of Ph3P (20 mol %) in toluene at rt (25 °C), but we obtained a
product 3aa in 45% yield after 24 h (entry 1). The yield (67%)
of the 3aa could be enhanced by using degassed toluene (entry
2). We wish to point out that we missed this point earlier and
had used 1 equiv of Ph
3P to get the maximum yield.
Satisfyingly, we isolated the α-carboline 3aa in 83% yield
(entry 3) after 36 h. Several other phosphines were screened,
but all of them were less e ﬀective (entries 4−7). Both electron-
poor phosphines [( p-FC
6H4)3Pa n d( p-ClC6H4)3P] and
electron-rich phosphines [MePPh 2 and ( n-Bu)3P] gave lower
yields compared to Ph 3P. Hence, we believe that optimum
electron density and steric factors around phosphorus are
crucial for this reaction. Further screening of reaction
conditions using di ﬀerent solvents (DCE, DMF, MeOH, 1,4-
dioxane, and H
2O; entries 8−12) revealed that toluene was the
best solvent for this annulation, providing 3aa in 83% yield
(entry 3). To further increase the yield, we performed a
reaction at a higher temperature (80 °C) but found a
completely di ﬀerent product 4aa (<10%) along with 3aa
(61%); we identi ﬁed product 4aa as the tosyl migrated and
aromatized carboline (entry 13) using analytical data (vide
infra). Inspired by this unexpected result, we performed several
reactions to obtain 4aa as the sole product by minimizing the
yield of 3aa. First, we tested a reaction by using Cs
2CO3 as an
additive; fortunately, 4aa was obtained in 75% yield (entry 14).
Other additives (K 2CO3 and tBuOK) were less e ﬀective
(entries 15 and 16) compared to Cs 2CO3.A tr o o m
temperature, the Ph 3P−Cs2CO3 combination did not give a
clear-cut reaction leading to either 3aa or 4aa (entry 17). Also,
low catalytic loading (10 mol %) of phosphine did not lead to
reactions eﬃciently (entries 18 and 19). Use of 50 or 100 mol
% of phosphine gave essentially the same yield as that from 20
mol % (entries 20 −23).
After establishing the best reaction conditions, we
investigated the scope and limitations of the [3 + 3] annulation
by using several 2-sulfonamidoindoles as C/N-donors and a
range of δ-acetoxy allenoates as 3C-synthons ( β, γ, δ-carbon
donor). As shown in Scheme 3 , regardless of the nature of
substituents (OMe, Cl, or CF
3) at the third/fourth position on
the phenyl ring of allenoate ( 2a−2e), good reactivity with
sulfonamidoindole 1a was achieved and the reaction a ﬀorded

in 75% yield. The δ-polyaryl-substituted allenoate 2g was
completely consumed to deliver 3ag in decent yield (72%). δ-
Thienyl- and indolyl-substituted allenoates 2h and 2i gave the
desired products 3ah and 3ai in yields of 73 −75%. Moreover,
this methodology was also achieved with aliphatic allenoate 2j
to deliver the [3 + 3]-annulated product 3aj in 71% yield.
Diﬀerent substituents on the nitrogen atom in the nucleophile
(1b−d) were well-tolerated a ﬀording high yields (73 −84%) of
3ba−3da. Finally, this methodology was also amenable with 5-
or 6-substituted sulfonamidoindoles ( 1e and 1f), providing
dihydrocarbolines 3ea and 3fa in good yields (74% and 71%).
Next, we explored the substrate scope involving δ-acetoxy
allenoates and sulfonamidoindoles in annulation and tosyl
migration cascade processes leading to products of type 4.A s
indicated in Scheme 4 , allenoates 2a−2d aﬀorded products
4aa−4ad in 70 −78% yields. To our delight, allenoate derived
from vanillin 2f and the heterocyclic allenoate 2h also provided
carbolines 4af and 4ah in good yields (68% and 64%,
respectively). δ-Methyl-substituted allenoate 2j reacted nicely
in the cascade process and a ﬀorded 4aj in good yield (68%).
Allenoate with naphthyl group at the ﬁfth position 2k also
showed decent reactivity with 1a to lead to the corresponding
product 4ak in 72% yield. Finally, N-substituted and 5-
substitiuted sulfonamidoindoles ( 1b and 1e) also a ﬀorded 4ba
and 4ea in decent yields (76% and 65%) with 2a. It is known
that Cs 2CO3 has fair solubility in many organic solvents and
quite low solubility in toluene, but the dramatic e ﬀect of tosyl
group transfer as observed here is rather unexpected. 15
Taking a cue from the reactivity of δ-acetoxy allenoates as
described above, we expected the formation of seven-
membered fused heterocycle using β′-acetoxy allenoates.
Thus, as depicted in Table 2 , we performed a reaction
between 2-sulfonamidoindole 1a (0.20 mmol) and β′-
acetoxyallenoate 5a (0.24 mmol) using the conditions shown
for entry 3, Table 1 . Surprisingly, we isolated product 6aa in
47% yield and identi ﬁed it as the [4 + 1] product via spiro-
annulation but not [4 + 3]-annulated product 7aa (Table 2 ,
entry 1). This result motivated us to investigate the [4 + 1]
annulation reaction in a systematic way for improving the yield
of 6aa. Increasing the reaction temperature from 25 to 80 °C
resulted 6aa in 69% yield (entry 2). Investigation of several
phosphines (entries 3 −7) indicated that ( p-tolyl)
3P was the
best choice as a catalyst (entry 7). We then screened other
parameters including solvent and additive. Solvent study
showed that toluene to be the best (entry 7); protic polar
and aprotic solvents (entries 8 −11) gave inferior results.
However, addition of Cs 2CO3 did not show any dramatic e ﬀect
in the reactivity (entry 12). Thus, conditions under entry 7
were found to be the best for this [4 + 1]-spiro-annulation.

substituents on the phenyl ring ( 5a−d) had no signi ﬁcant
eﬀect on this methodology, and spirocyclics 6aa−6ad were

To investigate the mechanism of tosyl migration cum [3 + 3]
annulation, we performed a few experiments. Heating
compound 3aa individually with (i) Cs
2CO3, (ii) Ph 3P, or
(iii) Ph3P+Cs2CO3 at 80 or 110 °C even for 36 h did not yield
compound 4aa (Scheme 7 a). Thus, it is likely that [3 + 3]
annulation with and without tosyl migration occurs by di ﬀerent
pathways. Also, in the absence of Ph 3P, we did not observe any
product at rt or at 80 °C( Scheme 7 b). The yield of 4aa
dramatically dropped when we used tosyl chloride as tosyl
cation source ( Scheme 7 c). Based on these experiments, we
infer that (i) the presence of Ph
3P is essential, (ii) temperature
and gradual addition of allenoate play a key role, and (iii) tosyl
anion (not cation) is most likely involved in the migration
leading to 4aa.

Plausible pathways for the [3 + 3] and [4 + 1] annulations
are shown in Scheme 8 . These divergent annulations may be
initiated through the phosphonium intermediate A1 or C1 via
the addition −elimination process between phosphine and 2a
or 5a. In the [3 + 3] annulation, the addition of 1a′ (generated
from 1a) to the phosphonium ion A1 at the δ-carbon gives
zwitterionic intermediate A2. Immediately A2 undergoes 1,4-
proton transfer and a ﬀords A3. Subsequently, A3 upon double
bond isomerization, 1,2-proton transfer, and phosphine
elimination leads to dienoate A6 via A4 and A5. Finally, A6
after intramolecular aza-Michael addition
6c yields 3aa. For the
formation of tosyl migration product 4aa, one possible
pathway is shown in Scheme 8 b. In this A1 undergoes a
second addition −elimination process with 1a′ to give the
allenic intermediate B3. Intermediate B3 is involved in the aza-
Claisen rearrangement 15,16a to give zwitterionic intermediate
B4. Finally, tosyl group elimination/readdition, and aromatiza-
tion involving species B4−B7 are expected to be involved in
the formation of the unexpected α-carboline with a tosyl
functionality at the γ-carbon 4aa. It is possible that the
nitrogen atom of intermediate B3 is electron de ﬁcient due to
the double bond and sulfonyl functionality. 15 Hence, one of
the double bonds of the allene moiety attacks this nitrogen to
deliver zwitterionic intermediate B4. Furthermore, at rt, proton

the two [3 + 3] leading to 3aa and 4aa annulations occur in
distinct ways. In the ( p-tolyl)3P-mediated [4 + 1] stereo-

selectively attacks at the γ-carbon of C1 to o ﬀer the ylide
intermediate C2. Then C2 is involved in 1,3-proton transfer to
produce C3. Finally, C3 undergoes addition −elimination
(SN2′-attack) leading to 6aa. It should be noted that in the
[4 + 1] spiro-carbo-annulation the key step is ylide formation
and the formation of the C −C bond is more favorable than the
C−N bond in the ﬁnal step. Although the possibility of the
formation of a 7-membered ring exists (cf. structure C3), we
have not observed it in the present study. Another possible
pathway (based on a reviewer ’s comment) for [4 + 1] spiro-
carbo-annulation is given in the Supporting Information
(Scheme S1 ).
The robustness of our divergent annulations is exempli ﬁed
by 1.0 mmol scale reactions of 1a with 2a or 5a under the
optimal conditions to a ﬀord 3aa, 4aa, and 6aa in high yields
(Scheme 9 ).
■ CONCLUSIONS
We have developed phosphine-catalyzed divergent annulations
that utilize β′/δ-acetoxy allenoates (as carbo-electrophiles) and
2-sulfonamidoindoles. In the temperature-dependent phos-
phine-catalyzed [3 + 3] annulations, δ-acetoxy allenoates act as
β-, γ-, and δ-carbon donors with 2-sulfonamidoindoles. At
room temperature, we obtained medicinally signi ﬁcant 1,2-
dihydrocarbolines in good to high yields. In sharp contrast,
tosyl migration and aromatization/cascade process occurred at
higher temperature (80 °C) to deliver α-carboline motifs with
tosyl functionality at the γ-carbon. In the stereoselective [4 +
1] spiro-carbo-annulation, 2-sulfonamidoindole acts as a 1C
synthon with β′-acetoxy allenoates to provide a novel class of
spirocyclopentene carboxylates with excellent diastereomeric
ratio (dr up to >20:1).
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
General Methods. All of the reactions were carried out either
under an inert atmosphere or in air. All required chemicals were
procured from Aldrich or local manufacturers and used as such
without further puri ﬁcation, unless noted. Melting points have been
recorded on MR-visual melting range apparatus and are uncorrected.
1H, 13C{1H}, and 19F NMR spectra were recorded using 5 mm tubes
on a 400 and 500 MHz NMR spectrometer [ ﬁeld strengths: for
13C{1H} NMR 400/100 or 500/125 MHz and for 19F NMR 400/376
or 500/470 MHz respectively] in CDCl 3 solution (unless speci ﬁed
otherwise) with shifts referenced to TMS ( 1H, 13C: = 0) or CFCl 3
(19F: = 0). Data for 1H, 13C{1H}, and 19F NMR are reported in δ
(ppm). All J values are reported in hertz. Infrared spectra were
recorded using an ATR technique on a FT-IR spectrophotometer.
Mass spectra were recorded using HRMS (ESI-Thermo Scienti ﬁc
EXACTIVE ORBITRAP/TOF analyzer) equipment. Crystallographic
data were collected on a X-ray di ﬀractometer system using Mo K α
radiation ( λ = 0.71073 Å) radiation. Structures were solved and
reﬁned using standard methods. Thin-layer chromatography was
performed on silica/alumina plates and components were visualized
under iodine/UV light at 254 nm. Column chromatography was
performed on silica gel (100 −200 mesh), for column elution process
hexane-EtOAc mixture was used as the eluent unless otherwise stated.
The starting materials 1a−g were prepared by using the procedure
of Kumara Swamy et al., 10c and 1h was prepared by the method of
Chang’s group. 17 Allenoate precursors 2a−k6c and 5a−g18 were
synthesized using literature procedures. Of these, 1a−e and 2a−j are
known; precursors 1f, 1h, and 5a−g are new. The solvent of
crystallization for all products was ethyl acetate −hexane (ca. 4:1 v/v).
